title: First words
goal: Greet people politely, say yes/no, please, thank you and sorry, and say goodbye the Odia way.
intro: Odia courtesy starts with **ନମସ୍କାର** (*nômôskarô*) and folded hands. In this unit you also meet the three words for *you* — the single most important politeness choice in the language — and the basic Odia sentence order: subject, object, verb.

vocab.note: Said with palms joined. Works at any time of day.
Also common, slightly less formal than ନମସ୍କାର.
Very Odia; used especially with elders and on the phone.
Add it to sound polite: ହଁ ଆଜ୍ଞା 'yes, sir'. Alone with rising tone: 'Sorry, what?'
Odias thank less often than English speakers among family and friends.
Usually the polite verb ending does the job; ଦୟାକରି adds extra politeness.
For elders, strangers, officials. Verb ends in -ନ୍ତି / -ନ୍ତୁ.
For friends, colleagues of your age, younger people.
Only for small children, very close friends — rude to strangers.
ମୁଁ ଅଛି, ତୁମେ ଅଛ, ଆପଣ ଅଛନ୍ତି. Negative: ନାହିଁ.
The usual way to take leave; saying ଯାଉଛି 'I'm going' is felt as inauspicious.
Formal/modern; ନମସ୍କାର is more common in speech.
ମୁଁ ବୁଝିଲି 'I understood'; ମୁଁ ବୁଝିଲି ନାହିଁ 'I didn't understand'.
Comes after the word: ମୁଁ ବି 'me too'.

grammar.title: Word order: subject – object – verb
grammar.body:
Odia puts the **verb at the end** of the sentence. The subject usually comes first, then the object or other information, then the verb: *I rice eat*.

There is often **no word for 'is/am'** when you say what something *is* (ମୋ ନାମ ଲିପି 'my name [is] Lipi'), but when you say how or where someone is, you use **ଅଛି** (*achhi*): ମୁଁ ଭଲ ଅଛି 'I am well'.

Question words stay where the answer would go — they don't move to the front: ଆପଣ **କେମିତି** ଅଛନ୍ତି? 'You *how* are?'

grammar.title: Three levels of 'you': ଆପଣ, ତୁମେ, ତୁ
grammar.body:
Odia verbs change according to **who** does the action and **how respectfully** you speak — never according to gender.

**ଆପଣ** (*apôṇô*) — respectful: strangers, elders, teachers, officials, customers. Verb endings with **-ନ୍ତି** (*-nti*); commands end in **-ନ୍ତୁ** (*-ntu*).
**ତୁମେ** (*tume*) — familiar: friends, siblings, colleagues of the same age, younger people. Verb ends in **-ଅ / -ଛ** (*-ô*).
**ତୁ** (*tu*) — intimate: small children, very close friends; to anyone else it is rude. Verb ends in **-ଉ / -ଛୁ** (*-u*); commands are the bare stem.

When in doubt, use **ଆପଣ**. Many Odias also use ଆପଣ-forms to parents and grandparents.

dialogue.title: Meeting a neighbour
dialogue.setting: Lipi, a college student, meets her older neighbour Mr Das in the lane outside her house.

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: ଭଲ ଅଛି, ଆଜ୍ଞା। ଆପଣ କେମିତି ଅଛନ୍ତି?
lines.roman: bhôlô achhi, agya. apôṇô kemiti achhônti?
lines.en: I'm well, sir. How are you?

lines.speaker: Mr Das
lines.native: ମୁଁ ବି ଭଲ ଅଛି। ଆସ, ବସ।
lines.roman: muṃ bi bhôlô achhi. asô, bôsô.
lines.en: I'm well too. Come, sit down.

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.en: Thank you, sir. But not now.

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: ଆଚ୍ଛା, ମୁଁ ଆସୁଛି। ପୁଣି ଦେଖା ହେବ।
lines.roman: achchha, muṃ asuchhi. puṇi dekha hebô.

culture: Odias greet with **ନମସ୍କାର** and joined palms; younger people may touch an elder's feet on special occasions. When leaving, people say **ଆସୁଛି** ('I'm coming [back]') rather than 'I'm going'. **ଆଜ୍ଞା** sprinkled into answers (ହଁ ଆଜ୍ଞା, ନା ଆଜ୍ଞା) is the easiest way to sound polite. Lord Jagannath of Puri is central to Odia identity, so **ଜୟ ଜଗନ୍ନାଥ** is heard everywhere — on phone calls, in shops and at the end of speeches.
